title: Undefined Behavior & C's Sharp Edges
relevance: Interviewers use UB to probe whether candidates understand that C compilers may delete safety checks and rewrite program logic under the assumption that UB never occurs.

phases.goal: Establish the four ISO C behavior categories and that UB means the standard imposes no requirements on the program.

must_hit.point: ISO C places program behavior into four buckets: well-defined, implementation-defined, unspecified, and undefined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four categories and contrasts that well-defined has a dictated result while the others leave choice or no requirements.

must_hit.point: Undefined Behavior is a state where the C standard imposes absolutely no requirements on the host environment or compiler; invoking UB invalidates the entire program's execution.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes or paraphrases 'imposes no requirements' and says the whole execution is invalidated, not just the bad operation.

must_hit.point: Implementation-defined behavior requires the compiler to choose from valid options and document it (e.g. int may be 16, 32, or 64 bits); unspecified behavior requires a valid choice but need not be documented and may change between compilations (e.g. evaluation order of g() vs h() in f(g(), h())).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates documented compiler choice from undocumented/unstable choice, with matching examples.

probes: What are the four categories of behavior in the ISO C standard, and what does Undefined Behavior actually allow the implementation to do?

hints.1: Start from how the standard classifies what your code is allowed to do.
hints.2: Contrast well-defined, implementation-defined, unspecified, and undefined—especially documentation and portability.
hints.3: UB means the standard imposes no requirements; implementation-defined must be documented (int size); unspecified need not be (argument evaluation order).

phases.goal: Show how compilers treat 'UB never happens' as an axiom to delete checks, prune ranges, and enable optimizations like vectorization.

must_hit.point: UB does not mean a predictable crash; the compiler may prove UB never executes and aggressively delete safety checks based on that assumption.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects 'UB equals crash' and describes deleted null checks or similar after a prior UB-producing access.

must_hit.point: In process(int *ptr) that dereferences ptr before checking ptr == NULL, NULL dereference is UB, so the compiler may assume ptr cannot be NULL and delete the if check entirely—UB effectively time-travels backward.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks dereference-then-check order and concludes the null check can be optimized away.

must_hit.point: With restrict on non-overlapping dest/src and signed loop index i, the compiler may drop overlap checks and assume i will not wrap (signed overflow is UB), enabling SIMD vectorization of the loop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions restrict as a no-alias promise and signed-overflow-as-UB enabling vectorized loads/stores.

must_hit.point: Compilers exploit UB via optimizations such as Value Range Propagation and Alias Analysis: states that would cause UB are treated as impossible, so branches can be proved unreachable and dead code eliminated.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names VRP/alias analysis or equivalent 'intersect with safe range / assume impossible' reasoning.

probes: Given a function that dereferences a pointer and only afterward checks for NULL, what can a modern optimizing compiler do, and why?

hints.1: Think about what the compiler is allowed to assume once any path would invoke UB.
hints.2: Order matters: an early dereference that is UB if ptr is NULL constrains later checks.
hints.3: Reading *ptr first makes ptr==NULL impossible in a valid program, so the if can be deleted as always false.

phases.goal: Connect C's UB model to the deliberate choice of raw speed over mandatory runtime trapping or weaker optimization.

must_hit.point: C was designed for OS and embedded work where boundary checks cost CPU cycles, so it assumes the programmer is infallible rather than mandating predictable runtime trapping like Java or Python.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States speed/hardware context and contrasts with languages that trap on errors.

must_hit.point: Aggressive UB-based optimization buys extreme execution speed; the rejected alternative is disabling those optimizations so explicit programmer bounds checks are preserved.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames speed vs keeping safety checks intact under weaker optimization assumptions.

must_hit.point: Unsigned integer overflow predictably wraps; signed integer overflow is UB—hardware differences in signed representation led C to leave signed overflow undefined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts wrap-around unsigned arithmetic with signed overflow as UB and the historical/hardware rationale.

probes: Why did C leave so much undefined instead of requiring traps or weaker optimizers, and what do you give up for that choice?

hints.1: Ask what C was built to run on and what each check would cost.
hints.2: Compare mandatory trapping languages with C's 'programmer is infallible' pact with the optimizer.
hints.3: Speed for OS/embedded vs Java/Python-style traps; keeping aggressive opts vs preserving bounds checks.

phases.goal: Apply catalog knowledge, defensive patterns, and tooling to detect and fix real UB (overflow checks, aliasing, bounds).

must_hit.point: Common UB includes signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free/double-free/dangling pointers, NULL dereference, reading uninitialized locals, strict-aliasing violations, data races, unsequenced modification (e.g. i = i++), invalid shifts, division by zero and INT_MIN / -1, out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic (even without dereference), misaligned access, modifying string literals, and calling through incompatible function pointers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several distinct catalog items with correct avoidances (check before arithmetic, NULL after free, memcpy/union for punning, one modification per statement, etc.).

must_hit.point: An overflow guard written as if (dist + 100 < dist) can be deleted because signed overflow is UB, so the compiler assumes dist + 100 cannot overflow and the comparison is always false; the fix is to check before arithmetic, e.g. dist > INT_MAX - 100.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why the wrap check is optimized to unconditional success and shows the pre-check form.

must_hit.point: Reading a float through a uint32_t* (or int*) cast violates strict aliasing; safely reinterpret bits with memcpy into an integer (or a union in C99+), which compilers can optimize to a register move.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects pointer cast punning and names memcpy or union as the safe approach.

must_hit.point: Catch UB with -fsanitize=undefined and -fsanitize=address, Valgrind, -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, static analyzers like clang-tidy/cppcheck, and defensive assert/limit idioms.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names UBSan/ASan as primary runtime injectors plus at least one of Valgrind, warnings, or static analysis.

probes: How do you safely reinterpret a float's bits as an integer in C, and how would you write an overflow check that an optimizer cannot delete?

hints.1: Avoid patterns the standard calls undefined, then check before you compute.
hints.2: Strict aliasing forbids float-as-int pointer casts; signed overflow forbids wrap-detection via overflowing adds.
hints.3: Use memcpy (or union) for bits; use dist > INT_MAX - 100 (or similar) before adding.

tradeoffs.topic: Mandatory runtime trapping (Java/Python-style) vs C's UB-as-no-requirements model
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Trapping would make mistakes fail predictably, but C targets OS/embedded contexts where boundary checks cost cycles; it assumes an infallible programmer and leaves the compiler free when rules are broken.

tradeoffs.topic: Aggressive UB-exploiting optimization vs preserving explicit safety checks
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Treating UB as impossible enables proofs that delete dead branches and unlock vectorization for speed; the alternative is weaker optimization that keeps the programmer's bounds checks even when they look unreachable under UB axioms.

tradeoffs.topic: Signed overflow (UB) vs unsigned overflow (well-defined wrap)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Unsigned wrap is predictable; signed overflow is UB because signed representations differ across hardware, so portable code must check limits before signed arithmetic rather than detecting wrap after the fact.

gotchas.trap: Treating UB as only 'unpredictable memory' because an out-of-bounds read happened to print a nearby variable on one machine.
gotchas.correction: UB means the compiler may unravel program logic entirely under the assumption you never write UB—not merely that memory contents are noisy.

gotchas.trap: Believing the compiler is malicious when it deletes a check.
gotchas.correction: The compiler only follows algebraic rules from the standard; deleting a branch it proved impossible is an optimization for speed, not intent-aware sabotage.

gotchas.trap: Placing safety checks after an operation that may already have invoked UB.
gotchas.correction: Once UB is in the past on that path, later checks can be assumed unreachable or constant-folded away; validate before the dangerous operation.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a test suite that only checks outputs because UB 'worked' today, especially under -O0.
gotchas.correction: UB can look like correct output until compiler version or optimization level changes (e.g. years of -O0 success breaking under -O3).
